newsitem.title: UK: Industry veteran Vallance led BT revolution.
newsitem.headline: Industry veteran Vallance led BT revolution.

text.p: For the chairman of British Telecommunications Plc, Sir Iain Vallance, the $22 billion takeover of MCI Communications Corp is a huge milestone in his 30-year career with Britain's main telephone provider.
Although BT was only privatised in 1984, Vallance had already been on the inside from 1981 when the company was first carved out of the state-run Post Office's telephony division.
Vallance's management career with the Post Office, in turn, stretches back to 1966 and gives him a depth of understanding of the modern communications market that is his trademark.
Known as a pragmatist, his view of the tangled, complex world of cable, mobile, data networks and regulation is clear and simple.

"The economics of telecommunications are straightforward," he told a recent newspaper interview. "You make your money by loading your network, so you want to get as much traffic across those networks as possible.
"The knack is then to provide (additional) services at prices that customers want".

While others in the industry have battled with internal personality clashes -- notably the 1995 spat at Cable & Wireless between chairman and chief executive that led to both men being pushed out -- Vallance had no such problems.
After flotation he stepped up to chief of operations in 1985, took on the chief executive's role in 1986 and the following year added the chairman's job to that one.
A year ago he handed over his chief executive's tasks to Sir Peter Bonfield in another smoothly-handled transition.
Unusually for a leaders in Britain's privatised utilities, Vallance has also kept clear of most of the "fat cat" flak aimed at his peer group.
And commentators have also praised the 53-year-old Scot's ability to keep a composed relationship, at least in public, with industry regulator, Oftel director general Don Cruickshank.
This summer saw a successful conclusion to BT's latest pricing regulation review, with Vallance welcoming the outcome as victory for logic.
Having steered the company through its British revolutions, he remains heavily engaged in pushing BT, and probably now the merged Concert company, towards a new technological phase.
He wants British regulators to allow BT to broadcast television down its networks so that it can master the "content" as well as the "carriage" and face down its cable competitors.
"The technology can do almost anything the imagination can think of, short of telephathy -- and we are working on that," he joked recently.
